transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-11 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Marta Lopez (Nimbus Eng Mgr), Samir Patel (Nimbus Backend), Jules Kim (Nimbus SRE)

Summary:
Quick sync on the recurring 5xx spikes over the last two weeks. Focus on correlation between client retry behavior and backend bursts, clarifying whether issues are server-side (runtime/backpressure) versus client-driven retry storms. Agree to tighten client retry spec, share filtered logs, and run a controlled harness.

Topics covered:
- 5xx pattern analysis and regional breakdown
- Client retry behavior and idempotency
- Circuit-breaker and backpressure thresholds on Redwood runtime
- Short-term mitigations vs. long-term guardrails

Action items (as discussed verbally, see metadata for structured list)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining; we got about 45, 48 minutes. Uh, quick rollcall, then Priya will run through the traces we pulled.
[00:12] Marta Lopez: Hi Alex, hi Priya. Marta here. Samir and Jules on my side as well.
[00:18] Samir Patel: Samir, hey.
[00:20] Jules Kim: Jules, hi.
[00:22] Priya Rao: Cool, thanks. So quick framing: last two spikes Nimbus saw — lots of 502/503/504s clustered around 10:30 and 14:10 UTC across eu-west-1 and us-east-1. We pulled request traces and matching Redwood runtime logs and tried to correlate with KV cache misses and model variant fallbacks.
[00:40] Samir Patel: And just to be clear, these were user-facing timeouts right, not internal job failures. We had clients reporting timeouts and then their SDK retried.
[00:48] Priya Rao: Correct. The pattern we think we see is: increased latency -> client retries -> sudden concurrency spike -> overload -> 5xx cascade, but there are a couple of traces that look like pure runtime OOM or kernel schedule delay.
[01:05] Marta Lopez: We definitely saw a couple of instances where our retry middleware did 5 backoffs in quick succession. I think the default sdk still does 3 immediate retries? The docs we had were ambiguous.
[01:17] Alex Chen: Right, that's a red flag. Our recommended client spec has historically been 2 retries with exponential backoff and jitter and idempotency header. Sounds like the SDK was using a more aggressive policy.
[01:28] Jules Kim: Also the logs show a few host-level GC pauses on the instance serving model-7b-quant. Could be unrelated but they align with one of the 14:10 bursts.
[01:40] Priya Rao: Yep, we flagged those. In a couple of traces we saw fallback routing to a lower-memory quant variant, but that added about 150ms and sometimes the client gave up and retried, compounding the problem.
[01:53] Samir Patel: So two hypotheses: client retry storm amplifies an already marginal capacity situation; or something in the model swap path is briefly blocking the serving threads which then produces 5xx.
[02:05] Alex Chen: Exactly. Today we want to: 1) agree on a short-term client retry spec for your SDK so retries don't amplify, 2) Priya will share targeted runtime traces, and 3) agree on alerts and circuit-breaker thresholds.
[02:17] Marta Lopez: Sounds good. For context our traffic profile is a mix of synchronous user requests and background batch embeddings; the spikes were mostly user-facing.
[02:27] Priya Rao: Noted. I'll screen-share the correlation sheet. (screen noise) So here, column A: timestamp, B: route, C: model_variant, D: 5xx code, E: client-retries observed, F: runtime_node. See row 42 — at 14:10 we had 48 requests with 3+ retries from the same customer token which saturated node-7.
[02:48] Samir Patel: Huh, 3+ retries from one session — our middleware should have hashed by session id and rate-limited, but looks like it didn't in this codepath. We'll dig in.
[02:58] Priya Rao: Also note row 47 where a fallback to model-7b-qnt-legacy caused a warmup of KV cache, increased latency by ~120ms and some requests timed out and then retried.
[03:12] Jules Kim: The 'KV cash' — sorry, kv cache — warmup on fallback is something we wanted to avoid. Do you have a warmup policy?
[03:19] Priya Rao: We have an option to pre-warm KV entries for pinned routes; currently not enabled for this org. We can enable a small warmup window for high-traffic routes to smooth swap latency.
[03:30] Marta Lopez: That helps. But immediate ask is the retry spec. Samir, can you confirm what SDK your team uses and whether it's custom?
[03:38] Samir Patel: It's our in-house middleware wrapping Redwood SDK, but we didn't enforce idempotency keys. It's basically default retry: 3 attempts, fixed backoff 500ms, no jitter.
[03:47] Alex Chen: That's the sweet spot for causing retry storms — fixed backoff leads to synchronized retries. We recommend exponential backoff with full jitter and limit to 1-2 retries for interactive calls. For async embedding/background, you can be more lenient.
[04:02] Marta Lopez: Ok so immediate change: Samir will change to 2 retries, exp backoff (base 200ms) with jitter, and add an idempotency token.
[04:12] Samir Patel: Yep, I can do that. We'll also add per-session bucketed throttling so one session can't create many concurrent inflight requests.
[04:20] Jules Kim: On our side we'll add an alert for 5xx >3% over 1m with tag filtering to avoid noise from batch jobs.
[04:28] Priya Rao: Regarding runtime side, we can tune the circuit-breaker threshold on the runtime to trip earlier for routes with high retried requests. There's a risk of failing fast and dropping user requests, but that may be better than cascade 5xx.
[04:40] Alex Chen: We'll propose conservative thresholds in the doc we share — e.g., open CB if error-rate > 8% for >30s and concurrency spike > 50% above baseline, with a gradual half-open policy.
[04:53] Marta Lopez: Can you also share the trace samples that show host-level GC? We want to rule out infra side issues.
[05:00] Priya Rao: Yes — Priya: will export filtered logs (only node metrics + request ids) and a small correlation sheet.
[05:08] Priya Rao: Also note one corner-case we found: the SDK's default connection pool sizing on customer side was 200. For synchronous user flows that's too high; with retries it created many parallel requests to Redwood.
[05:19] Samir Patel: We'll reduce pool to 50 for interactive routes.
[05:22] Marta Lopez: Good.
[05:24] (brief crosstalk)
[05:30] Jules Kim: Question: do you support per-route quota burst shaping so we can throttle at the platform edge rather than in our application?
[05:37] Alex Chen: Yes, Redwood Dedicated supports per-route quotas and burst windowing. For hosted we can provision soft limits and routing policies; we'll put recommended settings in the doc. For immediate POC, we can enable a soft-limit for the top two interactive routes.
[05:51] Samir Patel: If we enable per-route shaping, can we have a graceful 429 that includes retry-after so our SDK can respect it?
[05:58] Priya Rao: Absolutely — Redwood returns standard 429 with Retry-After header if configured. There's also the option of returning a 503 with Retry-After for transient service busy signals, if you'd prefer.
[06:09] Alex Chen: Important operational note: standard practice is prefer 429 + Retry-After for client throttling and 503 for internal degradation. But either works with a contract between parties.
[06:20] Marta Lopez: Understood. For the follow-up tests, what harness should we run?
[06:24] Priya Rao: We recommend two harnesses: 1) client-side deterministic retry pattern test — reproduce fixed-backoff vs exp-backoff and measure amplification; 2) stress test with model swap enabled to see KV warmup impact. We'll provide the harness scripts.
[06:38] Samir Patel: We'll run harness 1 first and share results. Expected timeline: by 2026-11-17.
[06:44] Jules Kim: On alerting, we need joint rules: Redwood will emit a trace-id tag when fallback occurs; can you ensure that tag is present in logs so we can filter?
[06:53] Priya Rao: Yes, we include fallback_variant and trace_id in structured logs; we'll make a filtered export for you.
[07:00] Marta Lopez: (notes) Also want to verify whether the 5xxs align with regional maintenance windows; I think there was a small host reboot but not during those spikes.
[07:08] Priya Rao: We checked infra events — no scheduled maintenance. The GC pause seemed to be application-level within the runtime.
[07:15] Alex Chen: Ok - recap of agreements: Samir will change SDK behavior to 2 retries, exp backoff + jitter, idempotency header, reduce pool to 50. Priya will share filtered runtime traces and a correlation sheet by Friday 2026-11-13. Jules will add alerting. Redwood will propose circuit-breaker thresholds/doc and provide harness scripts.
[07:36] Marta Lopez: Can you send a short doc with the recommended retry spec and suggested CB thresholds? That will help our infra team approve changes.
[07:42] Alex Chen: Yes — I'll send a one-pager with the spec and the link to the harness.
[07:46] Samir Patel: One more quick question — are there any suggested changes to model-variant fallback behavior to reduce latency during swap?
[07:52] Priya Rao: Two options: pre-warm KV entries for pinned routes, or return a short warmup-signal header so clients can choose to queue. Pre-warm will smooth things but uses a bit more memory; we'll outline tradeoffs in the doc.
[08:06] Jules Kim: Ok, that sounds reasonable.
[08:09] (wrap-up)
[08:11] Alex Chen: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule the deeper infra dive for the week of 11/22.
[08:20] Marta Lopez: Thanks.
[08:22] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings of product names (e.g., "KV cash"), speaker turns may be imperfect. Shared artifacts: correlation sheet link (internal): https://redwood.internal/poc/nimbus/5xx-correlation, harness repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/poc-harness (shortcuts).
